claims.text: Formal mathematical definitions of algorithmic fairness can be categorized into two broad families: those constraining decision effects on disparities, and those constraining protected characteristic effects on decisions.
Both primary families of formal fairness definitions typically yield strongly Pareto dominated decision policies analytically and empirically.
In college admissions, enforcing popular formal fairness criteria simultaneously reduces student-body diversity and class academic preparation relative to explicitly tailored policies.

For almost every collection of group-specific risk distributions with densities on [0, 1], no utility-maximizing threshold decision policy with optimal threshold 0 < t < 1 satisfies demographic parity or equalized false positive rates.
Excluding protected characteristics from risk models reduces aggregate and individual utility whenever those attributes carry predictive information.
Under path-specific fairness with full covariate conditioning, decision policies must be constant across individuals sharing non-causally affected covariates under mild structural conditions.
For almost every U-fine joint distribution, any feasible policy satisfying counterfactual equalized odds, conditional principal fairness, or path-specific fairness is strongly Pareto dominated.
Race-blind risk models systematically underestimate diabetes risk for Asian patients relative to White patients with identical age and BMI.
Gender-blind COMPAS scores overstate recidivism risk for women compared to men with equivalent criminal histories.

Equalizing false negative rates across racial groups in a complex medical care allocation algorithm reduces the number of enrolled high-cost Black patients from 205 to 113 compared to an unconstrained policy.

evidence.description: The authors categorize definitions into (1) those that constrain the effects of decisions on disparities, and (2) those that constrain the effects of legally protected characteristics on decisions.
Analytical proofs in Section 3 and 4 show that both families of fairness definitions result in strongly Pareto dominated decision policies.
Simulation of 1,000,000 college applicants shows constrained policies lie strictly below the Pareto frontier for student-body diversity and academic preparation.
Theorem 9 proves that no utility-maximizing decision policy satisfies demographic parity or equalized false positive rates for almost every collection of risk distributions.
Theorem 10 demonstrates that when conditional variance Var(r(X) | ρ(X)) > ϵ > 0, no blind policy is utility-maximizing.
Theorem 11 shows that for finite X under stated connectivity conditions, any Π-fair policy with W = X is constant across individuals sharing the same value of Z.
Theorem 17 proves using measure-theoretic prevalence that policies satisfying counterfactual equalized odds, conditional principal fairness, or path-specific fairness are strongly Pareto dominated.
NHANES data analysis shows applying a nominal 1.5% screening threshold under a race-blind model corresponds to a 1% threshold for White patients and a 3% threshold for Asian patients.
Broward County COMPAS data shows women with a COMPAS score of 7 recidivate at ~55% while men with a score of 7 recidivate at ~65%.

In the health care management dataset of ~50,000 patients, equalizing false negative rates yields 113 enrolled Black patients and 747 high-cost patients, whereas the unconstrained optimal rule yields 205 Black patients and 758 high-cost patients.

methodologies.name: Prevalence and Measure-Theoretic Analysis of Fairness Constraints
methodologies.description: Mathematical framework using infinite-dimensional topology and prevalence theory (shy sets) to analyze whether decision policies subject to formal fairness criteria are Pareto dominated.

methodologies.name: Empirical Policy Simulation and Calibration Analysis
methodologies.description: Simulation of constrained optimization problems via linear programming and subgroup calibration analyses on real-world decision datasets.
datasets: National Health and Nutrition Examination Survey (NHANES 2011-2018)
Academic hospital complex care management dataset (Obermeyer et al., 2019)
conditions: Binary decision rules with budget constraints b < 1 or b = 1

limitations.text: Proving Theorem 17 in the setting where utility u depends on both covariates x and outcome y remains an open problem due to underlying geometric complexity.
The structural conditions of Theorem 11 do not hold when counterfactual interventions induce deterministic constant shifts in covariates.
Formal axiomatic fairness definitions do not directly engage with substantive context-specific trade-offs or real-world policy consequences.

future_work.text: Extend Theorem 17 to general settings where utility u depends jointly on covariates x and outcome y.
Develop statistical and computational methods for mitigating measurement error, label bias, and sample bias when estimating causal counterfactual outcomes for algorithmic resource allocation.
Design preference elicitation and aggregation mechanisms to resolve policy trade-offs when arbitrating between competing decision algorithms.
